claims: "Eid Mubarak" is an Arabic phrase meaning "Blessed Eid" or "Blessed Feast/Festival".
"Eid Mubarak" is commonly used by Muslims as a traditional greeting during Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.
"Eid Mubarak" is the standard, most common greeting.
"Eid al-Fitr Mubarak" is specifically used to wish a blessed Eid at the end of Ramadan.
Eid al-Fitr is at the end of Ramadan.
"Eid al-Adha Mubarak" is used during the festival of sacrifice.
Eid al-Adha is the festival of sacrifice.
"Kul 'am wantum bikhair" is an Arabic phrase often added, meaning "May you be well with every passing year".
A response to "Eid Mubarak" is "Eid Mubarak to you too!".
A response to "Eid Mubarak" is "Taqabbal Allahu minna wa minkum".
"Taqabbal Allahu minna wa minkum" means "May Allah accept from us and from you".
Eid al-Fitr is breaking the fast.
Eid al-Adha is the festival of sacrifice.
Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha are the two major Islamic holidays.
"Eid Mubarak" is commonly exchanged after Eid prayers.
"Eid Mubarak" is commonly exchanged during visits to family and friends.
"Eid Mubarak" is commonly exchanged in text messages or social media posts.
Synonyms and similar phrases for "Eid Mubarak" include "Blessed Festival", "Happy Eid", "Blessed Celebration", and "Blessed Anniversary".
